The Torah.author: Traditionally Moses
The Torah.description: The Torah is the first five books of the Hebrew Bible: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers and Deuteronomy. It runs from the creation of the world through the lives of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, slavery in Egypt, the Exodus and the giving of the law at Sinai, ending with the death of Moses. Tradition counts 613 commandments in it; many modern scholars date its final form to around the 6th or 5th century BCE.
The Torah.significance: The Torah is the foundation of Jewish belief, law and identity, and every later Jewish text builds on it. Handwritten on parchment scrolls by trained scribes, it is read aloud in synagogues in weekly portions, completing the whole cycle every year.

The Prophets.author: Various; traditionally the prophets and others
The Prophets.description: The Prophets, or Nevi'im in Hebrew, is the second part of the Hebrew Bible. It has two sections: the Former Prophets (Joshua, Judges, Samuel and Kings), which tell Israel's history from entering the land to the Babylonian exile, and the Latter Prophets (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel and the Twelve shorter prophets). Much of the second section is powerful poetry.
The Prophets.significance: The prophets' calls for justice, care for the poor and faithfulness to God shaped Jewish and later Western ideas of morality. A passage from the Prophets, called the haftarah, is read in synagogue after the Torah reading on Sabbaths and festivals.

The Writings.author: Various; many unknown
The Writings.description: The Writings, or Ketuvim, is the third and final part of the Hebrew Bible. Its eleven books are very varied: poetry (Psalms, Song of Songs, Lamentations), wisdom (Proverbs, Job, Ecclesiastes), stories (Ruth, Esther), visions (Daniel) and history (Ezra-Nehemiah, Chronicles). Parts of Daniel and Ezra are in Aramaic, and dates for individual books are much debated.
The Writings.significance: The Writings show Jewish faith wrestling with suffering, love, doubt and survival, and they completed the Bible as Jews know it. Five short books, known as the Five Scrolls, are read on festivals, such as Esther on Purim and Ruth on Shavuot.

The Book of Psalms.author: Traditionally King David and others
The Book of Psalms.description: Psalms is a collection of 150 religious poems and songs, divided into five books. They include praise, thanksgiving, laments, pleas for help and songs for pilgrimage to the Temple in Jerusalem. Many carry headings naming David, but others name Asaph, the sons of Korah, Solomon and Moses, and scholars think the collection grew over centuries.
The Book of Psalms.significance: Psalms is woven through Jewish prayer, with many recited every day and others sung on festivals. Jews traditionally recite psalms for the sick, in times of danger and beside the dead, and the book has also shaped Christian worship and countless works of music and literature.

The Septuagint.author: Jewish scholars in Alexandria
The Septuagint.description: The Septuagint is the earliest translation of the Hebrew Bible, made into Greek for the large Jewish community of Alexandria in Egypt. The Torah was translated first, in the 3rd century BCE, and the other books followed over the next two centuries or so. Its name comes from the Latin for 'seventy', after a legend that about seventy scholars made it.
The Septuagint.significance: It allowed Greek-speaking Jews, and later the wider Mediterranean world, to read the Bible. It became the Old Testament of the early Church, and because it sometimes reflects Hebrew versions older than surviving manuscripts, scholars still use it to study the Bible's text.

The Letter of Aristeas.author: Unknown Alexandrian Jew, writing as Aristeas
The Letter of Aristeas.description: The Letter of Aristeas claims to be written by a Greek courtier of King Ptolemy II of Egypt. It tells how 72 Jewish elders, six from each tribe, came from Jerusalem to translate the Torah into Greek for the royal library, finishing in 72 days. Along the way it describes Jerusalem and the Temple and explains the reasons behind Jewish laws.
The Letter of Aristeas.significance: It is the earliest account of how the Septuagint was made, and its legend was retold by Philo, Josephus and the Talmud. It is also an early example of Jews explaining their customs to Greek readers as wise and reasonable, rather than strange.

The Wisdom of Ben Sira.author: Yeshua ben Sira of Jerusalem
The Wisdom of Ben Sira.description: This is a book of proverbs, advice and poems by a Jerusalem teacher named Ben Sira. It covers friendship, family, work, money, speech and the fear of God, and ends with a long poem praising Israel's great figures. His grandson translated it into Greek in Egypt, and large parts of the Hebrew original were rediscovered in the Cairo Geniza and at Masada.
The Wisdom of Ben Sira.significance: Ben Sira is one of the clearest windows into Jewish thought before the Maccabean revolt. It was left out of the Hebrew Bible, yet the Talmud quotes its sayings, and it is included as Sirach or Ecclesiasticus in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles.

The Books of Maccabees.author: Unknown; 2 Maccabees abridges Jason of Cyrene
The Books of Maccabees.description: These books tell the story of the Jewish revolt against the Greek king Antiochus IV, led by the priest Mattathias and his sons, especially Judah the Maccabee. 1 Maccabees was written in Hebrew but survives only in Greek; 2 Maccabees was written in Greek. They describe the persecution, the battles and the cleansing and rededication of the Temple in 164 BCE.
The Books of Maccabees.significance: They are the main historical source for the events celebrated at Hanukkah, though the famous story of the oil lasting eight days comes later, from the Talmud. They are not in the Hebrew Bible but are included in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles.

The Dead Sea Scrolls.author: Various; many linked to a group at Qumran
The Dead Sea Scrolls.description: The Dead Sea Scrolls are around 900 manuscripts, mostly in fragments, found between 1947 and 1956 in eleven caves near Qumran, by the Dead Sea. About a quarter are books of the Bible, including the complete Great Isaiah Scroll. The rest include rules for a strict religious community, hymns, commentaries and other writings, often linked to the Essenes, though this is debated.
The Dead Sea Scrolls.significance: They are the oldest known manuscripts of the Hebrew Bible, about a thousand years older than those known before, and they show how carefully its text was preserved. They also reveal the variety of Jewish life in late Second Temple times and are displayed today at the Israel Museum in Jerusalem.

Philo of Alexandria's writings.author: Philo of Alexandria
Philo of Alexandria's writings.description: Philo was a wealthy, learned Jew of Alexandria in Egypt who lived from about 20 BCE to 50 CE. His many surviving works are mostly commentaries on the Torah that read its stories as allegories, symbols of ideas about the soul and God, using Greek philosophy. He also wrote an account of his mission to the Roman emperor Caligula on behalf of Alexandria's Jews.
Philo of Alexandria's writings.significance: Philo was the first great thinker to bring Jewish scripture and Greek philosophy together. His works were preserved mainly by Christians and had little influence on the rabbis, but they are a key source for Jewish life in the ancient diaspora and for early Christian thought.

Josephus, The Jewish War and Antiquities.author: Flavius Josephus
Josephus, The Jewish War and Antiquities.description: Josephus was a Jewish priest and commander in Galilee who surrendered to Rome in 67 CE and wrote under Roman patronage. The Jewish War, in seven books, describes the revolt against Rome and the destruction of Jerusalem and the Temple in 70 CE. Jewish Antiquities, in twenty books, retells Jewish history from creation to his own day.
Josephus, The Jewish War and Antiquities.significance: Josephus is the main source for the fall of the Second Temple, for Masada and for figures such as Herod. His work was mostly preserved by Christians, and although his switch to the Roman side has long made him controversial, historians still rely heavily on him.

The Mishnah.author: Rabbi Judah the Prince
The Mishnah.description: The Mishnah is the first written collection of the Oral Law, the teachings the rabbis held had been passed down alongside the written Torah. It is arranged by subject into six orders covering agriculture, festivals, marriage, civil and criminal law, the Temple and ritual purity, with 63 tractates in all. It often records disagreements between sages rather than giving one answer.
The Mishnah.significance: After the Temple's destruction, the Mishnah gave Jewish life a portable structure based on study rather than sacrifice. It is the foundation of both Talmuds, is still studied daily in many communities, and its name, meaning 'repetition', reflects how it was learned by heart.

Pirkei Avot.author: Many sages; part of the Mishnah
Pirkei Avot.description: Pirkei Avot, often called Ethics of the Fathers, is a tractate of the Mishnah made up almost entirely of moral sayings rather than law. It opens with a chain of tradition running from Moses at Sinai through the prophets to the rabbis, then gathers short teachings from sages such as Hillel and Rabbi Akiva. A sixth chapter was added later.
Pirkei Avot.significance: It is the best-loved and most widely read part of the Mishnah, and many of its sayings have become everyday Jewish wisdom. It is printed in most prayer books and traditionally studied on Sabbath afternoons, especially between Passover and Shavuot.

The Tosefta.author: Traditionally Rabbi Hiyya; debated
The Tosefta.description: The Tosefta, meaning 'supplement', is a collection of rabbinic teachings that follows the same six orders and tractates as the Mishnah. It is considerably longer, adding extra rulings, explanations, stories and opinions that the Mishnah left out or stated briefly. Sometimes it seems to comment on the Mishnah, and sometimes it preserves different or older versions of the same teachings.
The Tosefta.significance: The Tosefta helps readers understand the Mishnah and how early rabbinic law developed. The Talmuds draw on similar material, and scholars value it highly for showing the wider range of opinions in the rabbis' world, though it has never been studied as widely as the Mishnah.

Mekhilta, Sifra and Sifre.author: Schools of Rabbi Ishmael and Rabbi Akiva
Mekhilta, Sifra and Sifre.description: These are the earliest rabbinic commentaries on the Torah's laws, known as halakhic midrash, meaning legal interpretation. The Mekhilta covers Exodus, the Sifra covers Leviticus and the Sifre covers Numbers and Deuteronomy. They go through the text verse by verse, showing how the rabbis drew laws from its exact wording, and they include stories and moral teachings too.
Mekhilta, Sifra and Sifre.significance: They show the method behind rabbinic law, linking the Oral Law directly to the words of the written Torah. They are quoted throughout the Talmud and later commentaries, and parts are known to many Jews today through the Passover Haggadah.

Targum Onkelos.author: Traditionally Onkelos, a convert
Targum Onkelos.description: Targum Onkelos is a translation of the Torah into Aramaic, the everyday language of many Jews in late antiquity. It is mostly close and literal, but it gently avoids describing God in human terms and adds brief explanations where needed. The Talmud links it to Onkelos, a convert to Judaism, though its origins are debated by scholars.
Targum Onkelos.significance: It became the authoritative Jewish translation of the Torah and is printed beside the Hebrew in standard editions. Jewish law encourages reading each week's Torah portion twice in Hebrew and once in Targum, and Yemenite Jews still read it aloud in synagogue.

Seder Olam Rabbah.author: Traditionally Rabbi Yose ben Halafta
Seder Olam Rabbah.description: Seder Olam Rabbah, 'The Great Order of the World', is a timeline of history from the creation of the world to the Bar Kokhba revolt in the 2nd century CE. In thirty short chapters it works out dates from clues in the Bible, such as ages, reigns and the length of the Egyptian exile, and adds rabbinic traditions for later periods.
Seder Olam Rabbah.significance: It is the basis of the traditional Jewish year count from creation, used on Jewish calendars and documents today. Its Persian period is much shorter than historians' reckoning, a difference that has long been discussed, but its dates remain standard in Jewish tradition.

The Jerusalem Talmud.author: Rabbis of the Galilee academies
The Jerusalem Talmud.description: The Jerusalem Talmud records discussions of the Mishnah by rabbis in the Land of Israel, mainly in the academies of Tiberias, Sepphoris and Caesarea. Despite its name it was not compiled in Jerusalem. It covers 39 tractates, including the agricultural laws, and is written in the Aramaic of Galilee. It is shorter and less polished than the Babylonian Talmud.
The Jerusalem Talmud.significance: It preserves the legal thinking and daily life of Jews in the Land of Israel under Roman rule. It was long overshadowed by the Babylonian Talmud, but it is especially important for farming laws in Israel today, and only one complete manuscript of it survives.

The Babylonian Talmud.author: Traditionally Rav Ashi and Ravina
The Babylonian Talmud.description: The Babylonian Talmud combines the Mishnah with the Gemara, centuries of discussion by rabbis in the academies of Babylonia, in modern Iraq. It is organised by Mishnah tractate and moves freely between law, debate, stories, medicine, ethics and folklore, often leaving questions open. Its standard printed edition has about 2,700 double-sided pages, each with commentaries around the central text.
The Babylonian Talmud.significance: The Babylonian Talmud became the central text of Jewish learning and the basis of Jewish law ever since. It is studied in yeshivas worldwide, and in the Daf Yomi programme hundreds of thousands of people read one page a day, finishing it every seven and a half years.

Midrash Rabbah.author: Various rabbis; compiled over centuries
Midrash Rabbah.description: Midrash Rabbah, 'The Great Midrash', is a set of ten separate collections on the five books of the Torah and the five Scrolls: Song of Songs, Ruth, Lamentations, Ecclesiastes and Esther. They gather sermons, parables, stories and explanations of verses. The collections were compiled at very different times, from Genesis Rabbah in late antiquity to Numbers Rabbah centuries later.
Midrash Rabbah.significance: Midrash Rabbah is the best-known source of the stories and lessons the rabbis drew from the Bible, many of which are now part of popular Jewish tradition. Preachers, teachers and students still turn to it when preparing talks on the weekly Torah portion.

Sefer Yetzirah.author: Unknown; traditionally Abraham
Sefer Yetzirah.description: Sefer Yetzirah, the 'Book of Formation', is a very short and cryptic text, only a few pages long. It describes how God created the world through 32 paths of wisdom: ten sefirot, here meaning basic numbers or dimensions, and the 22 letters of the Hebrew alphabet. It links the letters to parts of the universe, the year and the human body.
Sefer Yetzirah.significance: It is the earliest known Jewish text on the mystical structure of creation, and its idea of the ten sefirot became central to later Kabbalah. Major thinkers, from Saadia Gaon onwards, wrote commentaries on it, and it is still studied today by those interested in Jewish mysticism.

Hekhalot literature.author: Unknown; credited to Rabbis Ishmael and Akiva
Hekhalot literature.description: Hekhalot, meaning 'palaces', is a group of mystical writings describing journeys through seven heavenly palaces to the throne of God, inspired by Ezekiel's vision of the divine chariot. They describe guardian angels at each gate, secret names, and hymns sung before the throne. Famous rabbis such as Rabbi Ishmael and Rabbi Akiva appear as the travellers.
Hekhalot literature.significance: These texts are the main surviving evidence of early Jewish mysticism and helped pave the way for later Kabbalah. Some of their hymns found a place in prayer, and one, 'Ha-aderet veha-emunah', is still sung in some communities on Yom Kippur.

The piyyutim of Yannai and Kalir.author: Yannai and Eleazar ha-Kalir
The piyyutim of Yannai and Kalir.description: Piyyutim are Hebrew religious poems written to decorate synagogue prayers. Yannai and his successor Eleazar ha-Kalir, both of the Land of Israel, wrote hundreds for Sabbaths, festivals and fast days, full of rhyme, wordplay, alphabet acrostics and references to the Bible and Midrash. Much of Yannai's work was lost for centuries and rediscovered in the Cairo Geniza.
The piyyutim of Yannai and Kalir.significance: Their poems shaped the sound of Jewish prayer for over a thousand years. Kalir's poems are still recited on festivals and on Tisha B'Av, the fast mourning the Temple, and a poem by Yannai is sung at the Passover Seder.

The Passover Haggadah.author: Many generations; core from the Mishnah
The Passover Haggadah.description: The Haggadah, meaning 'telling', is the book used at the Passover Seder meal to retell the Exodus from Egypt. It includes the Four Questions, the Four Children, the Ten Plagues, blessings, psalms and songs such as Dayenu. Its core comes from the Mishnah, it took shape in the early Middle Ages, and some songs were added much later.
The Passover Haggadah.significance: It is often said to be the most printed Jewish book, with thousands of editions, many beautifully illustrated, such as the medieval Sarajevo Haggadah. Every year Jewish families around the world read it together, making it one of the most widely used Jewish texts.

The Masoretic Text and the Aleppo Codex.author: The Masoretes; Aleppo Codex by Aaron ben Asher
The Masoretic Text and the Aleppo Codex.description: The Masoretes were scholars, mainly in Tiberias, who fixed the exact text of the Hebrew Bible. They added vowel signs, chanting marks and margin notes counting letters and words, so nothing could be changed. The Aleppo Codex, made around 930 CE and corrected by Aaron ben Asher, is the most famous copy; much of it was lost after riots in Aleppo in 1947.
The Masoretic Text and the Aleppo Codex.significance: The Masoretic Text is the standard Hebrew Bible used by Jews today and the basis of most modern translations. Maimonides relied on the Aleppo Codex, and its surviving pages, now in the Israel Museum, are treated as one of the most precious Jewish manuscripts.

The Siddur.author: Rav Amram Gaon (first edition)
The Siddur.description: The Siddur, meaning 'order', is the Jewish prayer book for weekdays, Sabbaths and festivals. Its core includes the Shema, the Amidah and the Kaddish, many of which go back to ancient times. The first known complete version was written by Rav Amram Gaon of Babylonia around 870 CE, in reply to a request from Jews in Spain.
The Siddur.significance: The Siddur is the book Jews use most often, at home and in synagogue, and it has bound communities together across the world. Many versions now exist for different traditions, but they share the same basic structure that goes back to Rav Amram.

Halakhot Gedolot.author: Usually Simeon Kayyara; debated
Halakhot Gedolot.description: Halakhot Gedolot, 'The Great Laws', is one of the earliest books to arrange the laws of the Talmud in a practical, organised form. It follows the order of the Talmud's tractates but leaves out much of the debate, keeping the conclusions. Its introduction contains the earliest known list of the Torah's 613 commandments.
Halakhot Gedolot.significance: It helped make Talmudic law usable for communities far from the Babylonian academies. Later legal writers drew on it, and its list of 613 commandments started a long tradition of counting them, including Maimonides' famous critique and his own list.

Saadia Gaon, Tafsir.author: Saadia Gaon
Saadia Gaon, Tafsir.description: The Tafsir, meaning 'interpretation', is Saadia Gaon's translation of the Bible into Arabic, written in Hebrew letters (Judeo-Arabic). Saadia, born in Egypt and later head of the Sura academy in Babylonia, aimed for clear, natural Arabic rather than word-for-word translation. He avoided describing God in human terms and added explanations where needed.
Saadia Gaon, Tafsir.significance: It made the Bible directly understandable for the many Jews living in Arabic-speaking lands. It remained the standard translation in those communities for centuries, and Yemenite Jews still print it alongside the Hebrew and read it today.

Saadia Gaon, Beliefs and Opinions.author: Saadia Gaon
Saadia Gaon, Beliefs and Opinions.description: Beliefs and Opinions, known in Hebrew as Emunot ve-De'ot, sets out to prove that Jewish faith and reason agree. In ten sections it discusses creation, the unity of God, the commandments, free will, the soul, resurrection, redemption and how to live well. Saadia lists four sources of knowledge: the senses, reason, logical inference and reliable tradition.
Saadia Gaon, Beliefs and Opinions.significance: It is the first major systematic work of Jewish philosophy and set the pattern for later thinkers such as Maimonides. Translated into Hebrew in the 12th century, it is still studied as a classic statement of reasoned Jewish belief.

The Letter of Rav Sherira Gaon.author: Rav Sherira Gaon
The Letter of Rav Sherira Gaon.description: This is a long letter written by Rav Sherira, head of the Pumbedita academy in Babylonia, in reply to questions from the Jewish community of Kairouan in North Africa. They asked how the Mishnah, Tosefta and Talmud came to be written. Sherira answers by tracing the chain of sages and academy heads from the time of the Mishnah to his own day.
The Letter of Rav Sherira Gaon.significance: It is the earliest history of rabbinic literature and the main source for many dates and names of the Talmudic and Geonic periods. Historians and Talmud scholars still rely on it, even while debating some of its details.

Yosippon.author: Unknown author in southern Italy
Yosippon.description: Yosippon is a history of the Jews in Hebrew, covering roughly the Second Temple period and ending with the fall of Masada. Its anonymous author drew mainly on a Latin version of Josephus and on the Apocrypha. Over time it was wrongly believed to have been written by Josephus himself, which added to its authority.
Yosippon.significance: For centuries Yosippon was how most Jews learned about the Maccabees, Herod and the destruction of the Temple. It was among the earliest Hebrew books to be printed and was translated into Arabic, Ge'ez, Yiddish, Latin and English.

The Cairo Geniza documents.author: Thousands of writers, known and unknown
The Cairo Geniza documents.description: A geniza is a storeroom for worn-out writings that may contain God's name, which Jewish custom forbids throwing away. The geniza of the Ben Ezra Synagogue in Old Cairo kept about 400,000 fragments over nearly a thousand years. They include letters, contracts, court records, shopping lists and prayers, as well as lost texts such as the Hebrew Ben Sira.
The Cairo Geniza documents.significance: Brought to the attention of scholars largely by Solomon Schechter in the 1890s, the Geniza transformed knowledge of medieval Jewish life around the Mediterranean. It includes letters by figures such as Maimonides, and researchers in Cambridge and elsewhere are still studying it today.

Alfasi, Sefer ha-Halakhot.author: Rabbi Isaac Alfasi (the Rif)
Alfasi, Sefer ha-Halakhot.description: Rabbi Isaac Alfasi, born in North Africa and later a teacher in Lucena, Spain, wrote this summary of the Talmud's law. It keeps the Talmud's own wording but strips out the debates and topics not practised outside the Land of Israel, such as Temple and farming laws. It is sometimes called the 'Little Talmud'.
Alfasi, Sefer ha-Halakhot.significance: Alfasi's work became one of the three main pillars on which the Shulchan Arukh, the standard code of Jewish law, was later based. It is printed at the back of standard Talmud editions and is still consulted by students of Jewish law.

Rashi's commentary.author: Rashi (Rabbi Shlomo Yitzhaki)
Rashi's commentary.description: Rashi, a rabbi and winemaker of Troyes in France, wrote commentaries on almost the whole Bible and most of the Babylonian Talmud. His notes are short and clear, explaining the plain meaning of words and adding selected midrash. He sometimes translated difficult words into Old French, written in Hebrew letters, which today helps scholars of the French language.
Rashi's commentary.significance: Rashi is the essential companion for anyone studying the Torah or Talmud, and his commentary sits beside the text on every standard Talmud page. His Torah commentary was the first dated Hebrew book ever printed, in 1475, and a typeface is still named after him.

The Tosafot.author: Many rabbis, incl. Rashi's grandsons
The Tosafot.description: The Tosafot, meaning 'additions', are notes on the Babylonian Talmud by generations of rabbis in France and Germany, beginning with Rashi's grandsons, such as Rabbeinu Tam. They compare passages from across the Talmud, point out apparent contradictions and propose ways to resolve them. They often question or refine Rashi's explanations.
The Tosafot.significance: The Tosafot brought a new, sharp style of analysis that still defines advanced Talmud study. They are printed on the outer side of every standard Talmud page, opposite Rashi, and no serious student of the Talmud learns without them.

Solomon ibn Gabirol, Keter Malkhut and F.author: Solomon ibn Gabirol
Solomon ibn Gabirol, Keter Malkhut and F.description: Solomon ibn Gabirol was a poet and philosopher of Muslim Spain. Keter Malkhut, 'The Royal Crown', is a long Hebrew poem praising God, describing the universe as medieval science saw it and ending in a humble confession. Fons Vitae, 'The Fountain of Life', is a philosophical dialogue on matter and form; its Arabic original is lost and it survives in Latin.
Solomon ibn Gabirol, Keter Malkhut and F.significance: Keter Malkhut is recited in many communities on Yom Kippur. Fons Vitae was read by Christian scholars who thought its author, 'Avicebron', was a Muslim or Christian, until a scholar showed in 1846 that he was ibn Gabirol.

Bahya ibn Paquda, Duties of the Heart.author: Bahya ibn Paquda
Bahya ibn Paquda, Duties of the Heart.description: Bahya ibn Paquda, a judge in Muslim Spain, argued that Judaism includes not just outward actions but inner duties of the heart. His book is divided into ten 'gates', covering belief in God's unity, wonder at creation, trust in God, sincerity, humility, repentance, self-examination and love of God. It was translated into Hebrew as Chovot ha-Levavot in the 12th century.
Bahya ibn Paquda, Duties of the Heart.significance: It became one of the most loved books of Jewish ethics and spiritual life. It deeply influenced the 19th-century Mussar movement, which focused on building good character, and it is still studied today as a guide to the inner life of faith.

Judah Halevi, The Kuzari.author: Judah Halevi
Judah Halevi, The Kuzari.description: A philosophical dialogue built around the story of a king of the Khazars, a people of the Caucasus, who searches for the true faith. He questions a philosopher, a Christian and a Muslim, then a rabbi, whose answers fill most of the book. It is divided into five parts and argues that Judaism rests on shared historical experience, not abstract proof.
Judah Halevi, The Kuzari.significance: It became one of the best-loved defences of Judaism, especially after Judah ibn Tibbon translated it into Hebrew in 1167. It is still widely studied for its ideas about the Jewish people, the Hebrew language and the Land of Israel.

Judah Halevi, Songs of Zion.author: Judah Halevi
Judah Halevi, Songs of Zion.description: A group of Hebrew poems by Judah Halevi, one of the great poets of Muslim Spain, expressing longing for Zion, an old name for Jerusalem and the Land of Israel. Written in the polished style of Andalusian Hebrew poetry, they speak of a heart in the east while the body stays in the west. Halevi later set out for the Land himself.
Judah Halevi, Songs of Zion.significance: The poems turned a religious hope into personal, deeply felt verse, and shaped later Jewish love for the Land of Israel. His ode to Zion is still recited among the laments of Tisha B'Av, the fast mourning the destruction of the Temples, and a legend says he died at Jerusalem's gates.

Abraham ibn Ezra's commentary.author: Abraham ibn Ezra
Abraham ibn Ezra's commentary.description: Commentaries on most books of the Hebrew Bible, written by a Spanish scholar, poet and astronomer while he wandered through Italy, France and England. They focus on grammar, word meanings and the plain sense of the text, and are famously short and sharp. In places he hints, carefully, that a few verses may have been added after Moses.
Abraham ibn Ezra's commentary.significance: Ibn Ezra brought the language science of Muslim Spain to Jews across Europe. His commentary is printed in standard rabbinic Bibles and still studied today, and his cautious hints about authorship were later picked up by Spinoza and modern Bible scholars.

Abraham ibn Daud, Sefer ha-Kabbalah.author: Abraham ibn Daud
Abraham ibn Daud, Sefer ha-Kabbalah.description: A chronicle, whose title means 'The Book of Tradition', tracing an unbroken chain of teachers from Moses through the rabbis of the Talmud to the scholars of Spain. Written in Toledo, it includes the well-known story of four captive rabbis who were ransomed in different lands and founded new centres of learning.
Abraham ibn Daud, Sefer ha-Kabbalah.significance: Ibn Daud wrote it to defend rabbinic tradition against the Karaites, a movement that rejected the oral law. It remains a key source for the history of the Geonim, the heads of the Babylonian academies, and for the rise of Jewish learning in Spain.

Maimonides, Commentary on the Mishnah.author: Moses Maimonides
Maimonides, Commentary on the Mishnah.description: Maimonides' first major work, written in his twenties and thirties, explains the Mishnah, the early collection of Jewish law, chapter by chapter in clear, simple Arabic. It includes long introductions, among them his Thirteen Principles of Faith and 'Eight Chapters', an essay on ethics and the soul that introduces the tractate Avot.
Maimonides, Commentary on the Mishnah.significance: The Thirteen Principles became the best-known summary of Jewish belief and are sung today in the hymn Yigdal and recited as 'Ani Ma'amin' ('I believe'). Translated into Hebrew, the commentary is printed in many editions of the Mishnah.

Maimonides, Mishneh Torah.author: Moses Maimonides
Maimonides, Mishneh Torah.description: A vast code of Jewish law in fourteen books, written in clear Mishnaic Hebrew and arranged by subject. It covers everything from belief in God and daily prayer to Temple service, kings and the coming of the Messiah, including laws not practised in his day. It gives rulings without long debates or sources.
Maimonides, Mishneh Torah.significance: It was the first code to cover the whole of Jewish law, and its clarity made it both admired and controversial. Rabbis still study it closely, and it remains a foundation for later legal codes and a favourite text for daily learning.

Maimonides, Guide for the Perplexed.author: Moses Maimonides
Maimonides, Guide for the Perplexed.description: A philosophical work in three parts, written as a long letter to a student troubled by the gap between the Bible and philosophy. It explains that biblical descriptions of God with a body are figures of speech, discusses prophecy and creation, and gives reasons for the commandments.
Maimonides, Guide for the Perplexed.significance: It sparked fierce debate among Jews, and in the 1230s it was even burned in France, but it became the most important work of Jewish philosophy. Through Latin translations it also influenced Christian thinkers such as Thomas Aquinas, and it is still widely read.

Maimonides, Letter to Yemen.author: Moses Maimonides
Maimonides, Letter to Yemen.description: A letter Maimonides wrote from Egypt to Jacob ben Netanel, a leader of the Jews of Yemen, at a time of forced conversions and the rise of a false messiah there. It urges the community to hold firm, explains why the persecution would pass and warns against messianic claims and date-setting. He asked that it be read aloud widely.
Maimonides, Letter to Yemen.significance: The letter gave real comfort and is remembered with great gratitude by Yemenite Jews, who honoured Maimonides in their prayers. It remains a classic example of a leader guiding a frightened community, and of Maimonides' cautious view of the Messiah.

The Travels of Benjamin of Tudela.author: Benjamin of Tudela
The Travels of Benjamin of Tudela.description: A travel record by a Jewish traveller from Navarre in Spain who journeyed through southern Europe, Constantinople, the Land of Israel, Syria and Baghdad. City by city he notes the Jewish communities, their leaders and often their size, along with sights and trades. Accounts of the farthest lands, such as India and China, seem to be hearsay.
The Travels of Benjamin of Tudela.significance: It is one of the most valuable sources for Jewish life in the twelfth century, giving a rare picture of communities across three continents. Historians of the medieval world, Jewish and non-Jewish, still rely on it, and it was translated into many languages.

Sefer ha-Bahir.author: Unknown; traditionally Rabbi Nehunya ben ha-Kanah
Sefer ha-Bahir.description: A short, puzzling book of mystical teachings, written as sayings and answers between rabbis and arranged in brief paragraphs. Its title means 'Book of Brightness'. It speaks of God's powers as ten linked qualities, later called the sefirot, and uses parables of kings and palaces. It is traditionally linked to a sage of the first century, but first appeared in southern France.
Sefer ha-Bahir.significance: Scholars usually see it as the earliest work of Kabbalah, the Jewish mystical tradition, in the full sense. Its ideas, including a feminine side of the divine, became central to later Kabbalah and the Zohar.

Sefer Hasidim.author: Judah he-Hasid, with others of his circle
Sefer Hasidim.description: A large collection of short teachings and stories from the Hasidei Ashkenaz, a group of pious Jews in the Rhineland of Germany. It gives practical guidance on prayer, repentance, honesty in business, family life and dealings with non-Jews, often through real-life examples. It survives in a shorter printed version and a longer manuscript.
Sefer Hasidim.significance: It offers a rare window into the daily life and religious feelings of medieval German Jews. Its stress on inner devotion, humility and strict self-examination shaped Ashkenazi piety for centuries, and some of its customs are still kept.

Radak, Bible commentary.author: David Kimhi (Radak)
Radak, Bible commentary.description: Commentaries by David Kimhi of Narbonne in southern France, known by the initials Radak, on the Prophets, Psalms, Chronicles and Genesis. Clear and well organised, they explain grammar and the plain meaning of verses, often citing earlier scholars. He also wrote a Hebrew grammar and a dictionary of Hebrew roots.
Radak, Bible commentary.significance: Radak became one of the most read Jewish commentators and is printed in standard rabbinic Bibles. Christian Hebrew scholars also used his work, and it influenced translators of Protestant Bibles, including the King James Version.

Nachmanides' Torah commentary.author: Moses ben Nahman (Nachmanides, Ramban)
Nachmanides' Torah commentary.description: A commentary on the Five Books of Moses by a leading rabbi of Girona in Spain, finished after he moved to the Land of Israel late in life. It reads the text closely, often debating Rashi and Ibn Ezra, and draws on the Talmud and Midrash. It also includes brief hints to mystical meanings, which he calls 'the way of truth'.
Nachmanides' Torah commentary.significance: It was one of the first major works to bring Kabbalah into mainstream Bible study. Printed in standard rabbinic Bibles, it remains among the most studied Torah commentaries, valued for its depth and for its love of the Land of Israel.

The Zohar.author: Traditionally Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai; most scholars credit Moses de León and his circle
The Zohar.description: A large mystical commentary, mostly on the Torah, whose title means 'Radiance'. It follows Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, a sage of the second century, and his companions as they wander the Land of Israel and share secret meanings of scripture. It explores the inner life of God, the soul, good and evil. It first appeared in Castile, Spain.
The Zohar.significance: The Zohar became the central book of Kabbalah and, for many, a sacred text alongside the Bible and Talmud. Printed in Italy in the 1550s, it shaped prayer, customs and later movements such as Hasidism, and is still studied and recited today.

Sefer ha-Hinukh.author: Anonymous; traditionally attributed to Aaron ha-Levi of Barcelona (debated)
Sefer ha-Hinukh.description: A book, whose title means 'Book of Education', that goes through all 613 commandments of the Torah in the order they appear, following the weekly readings. For each it explains the source, the reasons behind it, its main laws and to whom it applies. The author, from Barcelona, says he wrote it to teach his young son.
Sefer ha-Hinukh.significance: Its clear, warm explanations made it a favourite way to learn the commandments for centuries. It is still widely used in schools and homes, and its search for the meaning behind each law has inspired later teachers.

Jacob ben Asher, Arba'ah Turim.author: Jacob ben Asher
Jacob ben Asher, Arba'ah Turim.description: A code of Jewish law, its title meaning 'Four Rows', written in Toledo by the son of a famous German rabbi who had moved to Spain. It covers only laws that apply after the Temple, divided into four parts on daily life and prayer, forbidden and permitted things, marriage, and civil law. It summarises earlier opinions before ruling.
Jacob ben Asher, Arba'ah Turim.significance: Its four-part structure became the standard way to organise Jewish law. The Shulchan Aruch follows it exactly, so its sections still frame the study and practice of Jewish law today. Jacob ben Asher is often simply called the Ba'al ha-Turim, 'author of the Turim'.

Gersonides, Wars of the Lord.author: Levi ben Gershon (Gersonides)
Gersonides, Wars of the Lord.description: A philosophical work in six books by a scholar of Provence who was also a mathematician and astronomer. It tackles the immortality of the soul, prophecy, God's knowledge, providence and the creation of the world. One long section on astronomy describes instruments and observations, including a measuring tool later called Jacob's staff.
Gersonides, Wars of the Lord.significance: It shows how far a medieval rabbi was willing to follow reason, and some critics mockingly called it 'Wars against the Lord'. Its astronomy was respected by Christian scholars too, and today it is valued in the history of both philosophy and science.

Shahin, Musa-nama.author: Mawlana Shahin of Shiraz
Shahin, Musa-nama.description: A long epic poem retelling the life of Moses, from the Exodus through the books of the Torah, written in Persian using Hebrew letters. Shahin wrote it in the style of classic Persian epics, mixing biblical stories with Jewish legends and Persian and Islamic tales. He also wrote poems on Genesis and other biblical books.
Shahin, Musa-nama.significance: It is the masterpiece of Judeo-Persian literature and was read aloud and copied in Iranian Jewish communities for centuries, often in beautifully illustrated manuscripts. It shows how Persian Jews made the Bible part of their own culture.

Hasdai Crescas, Light of the Lord.author: Hasdai Crescas
Hasdai Crescas, Light of the Lord.description: A philosophical work, in Hebrew Or Hashem, by a leading rabbi of Aragon who had lost his son in the anti-Jewish riots of 1391. It challenges Aristotle's physics, arguing for the possibility of empty space and of infinity. It also reorders the core beliefs of Judaism and stresses love and joy over pure intellect.
Hasdai Crescas, Light of the Lord.significance: It was one of the strongest critiques of Aristotle in the Middle Ages and a turning point in Jewish thought. Spinoza later drew on its ideas, and historians of science note how it anticipated modern views of space.

Joseph Albo, Book of Principles.author: Joseph Albo
Joseph Albo, Book of Principles.description: A work of Jewish belief, in Hebrew Sefer ha-Ikkarim, written in four parts by a Spanish rabbi who had defended Judaism at the Disputation of Tortosa, a long forced debate with Christian scholars in 1413–1414. It reduces Judaism to three root principles: the existence of God, divine revelation, and reward and punishment.
Joseph Albo, Book of Principles.significance: It was written to strengthen Jews at a time of pressure to convert, and its clear, readable style made it very popular. It is still studied as one of the main medieval attempts to define the core beliefs of Judaism.

Isaac Abarbanel's commentaries.author: Isaac Abarbanel
Isaac Abarbanel's commentaries.description: Long commentaries on the Torah and the Prophets by a statesman and financier who served the kings of Portugal, Spain and Naples. He opens each section with a list of questions, then answers them, often drawing on his experience of politics and courts. He also wrote works on the Messiah after the expulsion.
Isaac Abarbanel's commentaries.significance: Abarbanel tried to stop the 1492 expulsion of the Jews from Spain and then left with the exiles, and his writings carry their hopes for redemption. His commentaries are still read for their clear method and their interest in history and government.

Bovo-Bukh.author: Elia Levita (Elijah Bachur)
Bovo-Bukh.description: A verse romance in Yiddish about the knight Bovo and his love for the princess Druziana, full of adventures, disguises and battles. Elia Levita, a grammarian living in Italy, adapted it from an Italian version of the English tale Bevis of Hampton, writing in the Italian eight-line stanza. Christian elements were removed.
Bovo-Bukh.significance: It was one of the first popular works of Yiddish literature and was reprinted for centuries. It is often linked to the Yiddish phrase bobe-mayse, meaning an old wives' tale, though the origin is debated.

Solomon ibn Verga, Shevet Yehudah.author: Solomon ibn Verga, with additions by family members
Solomon ibn Verga, Shevet Yehudah.description: A history, whose title means 'The Rod of Judah', made up of accounts of persecutions of Jews from ancient times to the author's own day, including the expulsion from Spain. Ibn Verga, an exile himself, mixes historical reports with imagined conversations between kings, scholars and Jews about why the Jews are hated.
Solomon ibn Verga, Shevet Yehudah.significance: It was one of the first Jewish attempts to explain persecution through human causes as well as divine will. Widely read and translated, it shaped how later generations remembered the Spanish expulsion and is still read by historians today.

Samuel Usque, Consolation for the Tribul.author: Samuel Usque
Samuel Usque, Consolation for the Tribul.description: A history of the Jewish people written as a conversation between three shepherds, one of whom stands for Jacob, or Israel. Across three dialogues it moves from biblical times through the Second Temple to the persecutions of Usque's own century, including Spain and Portugal. It was printed in Ferrara, Italy.
Samuel Usque, Consolation for the Tribul.significance: It was written for conversos, Jews forced into Christianity who were returning to Judaism, to help them understand their history and keep hope. It is a moving record of the Iberian Jewish exile and a landmark of Jewish writing in Portuguese.

The Ferrara Bible.author: Abraham Usque and Yom Tov Atias (publishers)
The Ferrara Bible.description: A complete translation of the Hebrew Bible into Spanish, printed in Ferrara, Italy. It follows the Hebrew word by word, using the traditional Judeo-Spanish style of translation taught in Jewish schools in Spain. It was printed in Latin letters so that former conversos, who could not read Hebrew, could use it.
The Ferrara Bible.significance: It gave Spanish-speaking Jews scattered after the expulsions a Bible in their own language. It became the standard Jewish Spanish Bible for generations, and versions were also prepared for Christian readers. It influenced later Spanish translations and is remembered as a landmark of Sephardi culture.

Joseph Karo, Shulchan Aruch.author: Joseph Karo
Joseph Karo, Shulchan Aruch.description: A short code of Jewish law, its title meaning 'Set Table', written in Safed in the Land of Israel by a rabbi born in Spain. It follows the four-part structure of the Arba'ah Turim and gives clear, brief rulings, based on his larger work Beit Yosef. It mostly follows Sephardi custom.
Joseph Karo, Shulchan Aruch.significance: With the notes of Moses Isserles, it became the most widely accepted code of Jewish law. It is still the starting point for questions of practice, and it is surrounded in print by many layers of later commentary.

Moses Isserles, the Mapah.author: Moses Isserles (Rema)
Moses Isserles, the Mapah.description: Short notes, whose name means 'The Tablecloth', added by Moses Isserles of Kraków to the Shulchan Aruch, the 'Set Table'. Wherever Ashkenazi custom differs from Joseph Karo's Sephardi rulings, Isserles adds the Ashkenazi practice. The notes are printed within the text itself in a different typeface.
Moses Isserles, the Mapah.significance: His notes made the Shulchan Aruch acceptable to Ashkenazi Jews, turning it into a shared code for Jews across the world. Ashkenazi Jews today still generally follow his rulings, often simply quoting 'the Rema', the name formed from his initials.

Ein Yaakov.author: Jacob ibn Habib, completed by his son Levi ibn Habib
Ein Yaakov.description: A collection of the aggadah, the stories, legends, sayings and moral teachings, of the Talmud, arranged in the order of the Talmud's tractates and leaving out the legal debates. It was compiled by a Spanish exile in Salonika and comes with his own commentary, and later editions added more.
Ein Yaakov.significance: It made the warmer, story-telling side of the Talmud open to ordinary readers. For centuries, study groups in synagogues read it together, and it is still widely printed and studied, often as a gentle way into Talmud learning.

Azariah dei Rossi, Me'or Einayim.author: Azariah dei Rossi
Azariah dei Rossi, Me'or Einayim.description: A work, whose title means 'Light of the Eyes', by an Italian Jewish scholar, prompted by the 1570 earthquake in Ferrara. It examines Jewish history using Greek and Latin writers, Philo, Josephus and Church sources alongside rabbinic texts, and questions some traditional dates and stories.
Azariah dei Rossi, Me'or Einayim.significance: It is often seen as the start of critical Jewish history. Some rabbis of the time restricted its reading, but modern scholars treat it as a pioneering work that brought Renaissance methods into Jewish study.

Chaim Vital, Etz Chaim.author: Chaim Vital
Chaim Vital, Etz Chaim.description: The main record of the teachings of Isaac Luria, known as the Ari, a mystic of Safed who wrote little himself. Its title means 'Tree of Life'. It sets out a detailed system of how creation began with God's withdrawal, how divine vessels shattered, and how people help repair the world through prayer and good deeds.
Chaim Vital, Etz Chaim.significance: Lurianic Kabbalah became the dominant form of Jewish mysticism and shaped later movements, including Hasidism. The idea of repair, or tikkun, is still widely used today, though often in a much broader sense of making the world better. The book is still studied by kabbalists today.

The Lekhah Dodi and Safed prayers.author: Shlomo Halevi Alkabetz and the Safed kabbalists
The Lekhah Dodi and Safed prayers.description: A hymn and a set of prayers created by the mystics of Safed to welcome the Sabbath on Friday evening. Lekhah Dodi, 'Come, my beloved', greets the Sabbath as a bride and queen, and the first letters of its verses spell the author's name. The service also includes psalms the mystics sang as they went out to greet the Sabbath.
The Lekhah Dodi and Safed prayers.significance: This Friday-night service, known as Kabbalat Shabbat, spread from Safed to almost every Jewish community. Lekhah Dodi is sung to countless melodies today, and the congregation turns to the door to welcome the Sabbath at its final verse.

Tsene-rene.author: Jacob ben Isaac Ashkenazi of Janów
Tsene-rene.description: A Yiddish retelling of the weekly Torah readings and other biblical books, woven together with Midrash, legends and moral lessons. Its name comes from a verse in the Song of Songs meaning 'Go out and see'. The earliest surviving edition dates from 1622; earlier ones are lost. It was written for readers without Hebrew, especially women, and is told in a warm, homely style.
Tsene-rene.significance: It became one of the most popular Jewish books ever, read on the Sabbath in Ashkenazi homes for about three centuries. It shaped how generations of Jewish women knew the Bible, and it is still printed today.

The Maharal of Prague's works.author: Judah Loew ben Bezalel (the Maharal)
The Maharal of Prague's works.description: A body of books by Judah Loew, chief rabbi of Prague, including a commentary on Rashi and works on exile and redemption, the Torah and ethics. Written in a dense, original style, they explore the inner meaning of Jewish ideas and stories, and he also called for better methods of teaching children.
The Maharal of Prague's works.significance: The Maharal shaped later Jewish thought, including Hasidism and Rav Kook. He is famous through the later legend that he made a golem, a clay figure brought to life, though that story only appears long after his death.

David Gans, Tzemach David.author: David Gans
David Gans, Tzemach David.description: A chronicle by a Prague scholar, astronomer and student of the Maharal, in two parts: one on Jewish history and one on world history, each set out year by year. Gans used both Jewish and non-Jewish sources and knew the astronomers Tycho Brahe and Johannes Kepler.
David Gans, Tzemach David.significance: It was one of the first Jewish works to place Jewish history alongside the history of the wider world. It was widely read and reprinted, and it is valued today as a sign of Jewish openness to science and learning in Renaissance Prague.

Isaiah Horowitz, Shnei Luchot HaBrit.author: Isaiah Horowitz (the Shelah)
Isaiah Horowitz, Shnei Luchot HaBrit.description: A large guide to Jewish life whose title means 'The Two Tablets of the Covenant', known by its initials as the Shelah. It joins law, ethics and Kabbalah, covering the commandments, the festivals and daily conduct. The author completed it in the Land of Israel after leaving Prague, and his son published it.
Isaiah Horowitz, Shnei Luchot HaBrit.significance: It spread Kabbalistic ideas and customs into everyday Ashkenazi practice and was widely read as a book of moral guidance. A prayer from it for one's children is still recited by many families before the festival of Shavuot.

Menasseh ben Israel, The Hope of Israel.author: Menasseh ben Israel
Menasseh ben Israel, The Hope of Israel.description: A short book by an Amsterdam rabbi and printer, responding to a report that some lost tribes of Israel had been found in South America. It argues that the Messiah will come once the Jews are scattered to every corner of the earth. It was quickly translated into English and dedicated to the English Parliament.
Menasseh ben Israel, The Hope of Israel.significance: It opened the way for Menasseh's mission to Oliver Cromwell, asking that Jews be allowed back in England, from which they had been expelled in 1290. No formal law followed, but Jews were quietly permitted to settle from 1656.

Spinoza, Theological-Political Treatise.author: Baruch Spinoza
Spinoza, Theological-Political Treatise.description: A book, published anonymously in Amsterdam, by a philosopher who had been expelled from the city's Jewish community in 1656. In twenty chapters it argues that the Bible should be studied like any other historical text, questions whether Moses wrote the whole Torah, and defends freedom of thought and speech.
Spinoza, Theological-Political Treatise.significance: It was banned and condemned widely in its time, yet it laid foundations for modern Bible criticism and for ideas of free speech and secular government. It remains a turning point in debates about Judaism and the modern world.

The memoirs of Glikl of Hamelin.author: Glikl of Hamelin
The memoirs of Glikl of Hamelin.description: A memoir in seven books written by a Jewish businesswoman from Hamburg, begun after the death of her husband to ease her grief and to tell her children about their family. It mixes family history, business dealings, travel, moral tales and religious reflection. She wrote it as a widow raising a large family while running the family trade.
The memoirs of Glikl of Hamelin.significance: It is one of the earliest known memoirs by a Jewish woman and a rare first-hand view of Jewish family and commercial life in 17th-century Germany. First printed in 1896, it is now widely translated and read by historians and general readers alike.

Me'am Lo'ez.author: Yaakov Culi, continued by others
Me'am Lo'ez.description: A huge commentary on the Bible written in Ladino, the Judeo-Spanish language of Sephardi Jews. Rabbi Yaakov Culi of Constantinople began it with Genesis, and after his death other scholars carried on the work. It goes through the text verse by verse, weaving in law, stories, history and moral advice drawn from the Talmud and later teachers.
Me'am Lo'ez.significance: It brought traditional Jewish learning to Sephardi families who could not read Hebrew, and was read aloud in homes and synagogues across the Ottoman world. It is remembered as the best-loved book of Ladino literature and has since been translated into Hebrew and English.

Ramchal, Mesillat Yesharim.author: Moshe Chaim Luzzatto (Ramchal)
Ramchal, Mesillat Yesharim.description: A short book on how to become a better person, written by the Italian rabbi, poet and mystic Moshe Chaim Luzzatto. Its title means The Path of the Just. It follows a ladder of qualities taken from the Talmud, starting with watchfulness and zeal and climbing step by step towards holiness, explaining each trait and what gets in its way.
Ramchal, Mesillat Yesharim.significance: It became the most widely studied Jewish book on character and inner life, especially in the Musar movement of Lithuanian yeshivas. It remains a standard text in yeshivas and study groups today, valued for its clear, practical structure.

Toledot Yaakov Yosef.author: Yaakov Yosef of Polonne
Toledot Yaakov Yosef.description: A collection of sermons arranged by the weekly Torah readings, written by a leading disciple of the Baal Shem Tov, the founder of Hasidism. Again and again it passes on teachings with the words heard from my teacher, preserving many of the Baal Shem Tov's own sayings. It also criticises scholars and leaders who were cut off from ordinary people.
Toledot Yaakov Yosef.significance: It was the first Hasidic book ever printed, and it carried the new movement's ideas far beyond the circle of its founder. It provoked strong opposition at the time and is still a key source for anyone studying the Baal Shem Tov and early Hasidism.

Moses Mendelssohn, Jerusalem and his Tor.author: Moses Mendelssohn
Moses Mendelssohn, Jerusalem and his Tor.description: Two works by the Berlin philosopher Moses Mendelssohn. His translation of the Torah rendered the text into German printed in Hebrew letters, with a Hebrew commentary written by him and other scholars. Jerusalem is a book of philosophy arguing for freedom of conscience, the separation of religion and state, and the view that Judaism asks for deeds rather than forced beliefs.
Moses Mendelssohn, Jerusalem and his Tor.significance: Together they helped open the Haskalah, the Jewish Enlightenment, by bringing Jews into German language and European thought while keeping Jewish practice. They are remembered as a turning point between traditional and modern Jewish life, praised by some and blamed by others for what followed.

Shneur Zalman of Liadi, Tanya.author: Shneur Zalman of Liadi
Shneur Zalman of Liadi, Tanya.description: The central work of Chabad Hasidism, also called Likutei Amarim. It explains the inner life of the soul and the struggle between a person's good and selfish sides. It focuses on the ordinary person in between, who may never be perfect but can still control thought, speech and action, and it sets out a path of serving God through both mind and heart.
Shneur Zalman of Liadi, Tanya.significance: It gave Hasidism a systematic philosophy and became the foundation of the Chabad movement. Chabad followers study a portion every day, and it has been printed many thousands of times in towns and cities around the world.

Rebbe Nachman of Breslov, Likutei Mohara.author: Nachman of Breslov (recorded by Nathan of Nemirov)
Rebbe Nachman of Breslov, Likutei Mohara.description: Likutei Moharan is a large collection of Rebbe Nachman's teachings, written down by his student Nathan of Nemirov. It covers joy, faith, prayer, and speaking to God in one's own words. The Tales are thirteen mystical stories, printed side by side in Hebrew and Yiddish, including The Lost Princess and The Seven Beggars.
Rebbe Nachman of Breslov, Likutei Mohara.significance: They are the core texts of Breslov Hasidism, a movement that has had no living rebbe since Nachman died in 1810. The stories are also admired outside religious circles as early modern Jewish fiction and have influenced writers and thinkers into the present day.

Chaim of Volozhin, Nefesh HaChaim.author: Chaim of Volozhin
Chaim of Volozhin, Nefesh HaChaim.description: A work of religious philosophy by the leading student of the Vilna Gaon, published after the author's death. It teaches that human actions affect the spiritual worlds, and places the study of Torah for its own sake at the very centre of religious life. It also answers some ideas of the growing Hasidic movement.
Chaim of Volozhin, Nefesh HaChaim.significance: Its author founded the Volozhin yeshiva, the model for the great Lithuanian yeshivas, and this book became their guiding philosophy. It is still studied in yeshivas today as the classic statement of the value of Torah study.

Samson Raphael Hirsch, Nineteen Letters.author: Samson Raphael Hirsch
Samson Raphael Hirsch, Nineteen Letters.description: A short book written as nineteen letters from a young rabbi to a friend troubled by doubts about Judaism. It argues that the Torah is a complete and meaningful way of life, fully compatible with taking part in modern society. It was first published under a pen name, Ben Uziel.
Samson Raphael Hirsch, Nineteen Letters.significance: It set out the outlook later known as Torah with worldly life, which became a founding idea of modern Orthodox Judaism in Germany and beyond. It is still read as a clear defence of traditional Judaism in a modern world.

Abraham Mapu, Love of Zion.author: Abraham Mapu
Abraham Mapu, Love of Zion.description: A romantic novel set in ancient Israel in the days of the prophet Isaiah. It tells a love story full of family secrets, villains and coincidences, against a vivid picture of the hills and towns of the Land of Israel. It was written in a biblical style of Hebrew, as modern Hebrew did not yet exist.
Abraham Mapu, Love of Zion.significance: It is counted as the first modern Hebrew novel and was a great success among young Jews in Eastern Europe. For many readers it stirred a longing for the Land of Israel and showed that Hebrew could be used for modern storytelling.

Heinrich Graetz, History of the Jews.author: Heinrich Graetz
Heinrich Graetz, History of the Jews.description: A history of the Jewish people from biblical times to the 19th century, published in eleven volumes. It draws on a wide range of sources and is told with strong opinions and a gift for storytelling. It was later translated into English, Hebrew and other languages.
Heinrich Graetz, History of the Jews.significance: It was the first full modern history of the Jews and shaped how generations understood their own past. Historians now point out its biases and its neglect of some communities, but it remains a landmark of modern Jewish scholarship and is still consulted today.

Moses Hess, Rome and Jerusalem.author: Moses Hess
Moses Hess, Rome and Jerusalem.description: A book written as a series of letters by a German Jewish socialist who had once favoured assimilation. Inspired by the Italian struggle for unity, it argues that the Jews are a nation and that they should build a society of their own in the Land of Israel. It also criticises those who abandoned Jewish identity.
Moses Hess, Rome and Jerusalem.significance: Little noticed in its own day, it is now seen as one of the earliest works of modern Zionism. Herzl later wrote that it had already expressed many of his own ideas years before him, and it is still read as an early Zionist classic.

Shlomo Ganzfried, Kitzur Shulchan Aruch.author: Shlomo Ganzfried
Shlomo Ganzfried, Kitzur Shulchan Aruch.description: A short summary of everyday Jewish law, based on the larger Shulchan Aruch. It covers prayer, blessings, Sabbath, festivals, kosher food, family life and mourning, in simple Hebrew and short numbered paragraphs. It was written for ordinary people rather than scholars, so that any reader could look up what to do in daily life.
Shlomo Ganzfried, Kitzur Shulchan Aruch.significance: It became one of the most popular Jewish books ever printed and was found in countless homes. It is still widely used and translated, though many now rely on later and more detailed guides for practical rulings.

Mendele Mocher Sforim, The Travels of Be.author: Mendele Mocher Sforim (S. Y. Abramovitsh)
Mendele Mocher Sforim, The Travels of Be.description: A comic novel about Benjamin, a dreamy man from a poor shtetl, who sets off with his friend Senderl to find the lost tribes and the Land of Israel. They never get far from home. The story is often compared to Don Quixote and pokes fun at the poverty and helplessness of shtetl life.
Mendele Mocher Sforim, The Travels of Be.significance: Its author is called the grandfather of modern Yiddish literature, and this is one of his best-known works. It is still read as a sharp and funny portrait of Eastern European Jewish life in the 19th century.

Leon Pinsker, Auto-Emancipation.author: Leon Pinsker
Leon Pinsker, Auto-Emancipation.description: A pamphlet by a Russian Jewish doctor, written after the pogroms of 1881 and first published anonymously. It argues that hatred of Jews is a deep-rooted illness that equal rights alone cannot cure. Its answer is that Jews must free themselves by gaining a land of their own.
Leon Pinsker, Auto-Emancipation.significance: It was one of the first calls for a Jewish homeland and inspired the Hovevei Zion (Lovers of Zion) movement, which Pinsker went on to lead. It is remembered as a key step towards political Zionism.

Naftali Herz Imber, Hatikvah.author: Naftali Herz Imber
Naftali Herz Imber, Hatikvah.description: A Hebrew poem first called Tikvateinu, meaning Our Hope, by a wandering poet from Galicia. It speaks of the Jewish longing to return as a free people to the Land of Israel. Its opening verses were later set to a tune based on a European folk melody.
Naftali Herz Imber, Hatikvah.significance: It was sung by early Zionist settlers and adopted as the anthem of the Zionist movement. It became the national anthem of Israel, formally confirmed in law in 2004, and is sung at Jewish events around the world.

Emma Lazarus, The New Colossus.author: Emma Lazarus
Emma Lazarus, The New Colossus.description: A sonnet by a Jewish American poet from New York, written to help raise money for the base of the Statue of Liberty. It imagines the statue as a mother of exiles, welcoming the poor and the persecuted to America. Lazarus had been moved by the plight of Jewish refugees from Russia.
Emma Lazarus, The New Colossus.significance: In 1903 it was placed on a plaque inside the statue's base, and its words became a symbol of America as a land of refuge. It is remembered as one of the most famous poems in American life, written by a pioneering Jewish voice.

I. L. Peretz, short stories.author: I. L. Peretz
I. L. Peretz, short stories.description: Short stories by a Warsaw writer, ranging from realistic tales of poverty to reworked Hasidic and folk stories. Among the best known are Bontshe the Silent, about a man who suffers without complaint, and If Not Higher, about a rabbi's secret good deeds. They are often ironic, warm and gently questioning.
I. L. Peretz, short stories.significance: Peretz is counted among the three classic founders of modern Yiddish literature, and his home in Warsaw was a centre for young writers. His stories helped turn Yiddish into a serious literary language and are still read and taught today.

Ahad Ha'am's essays.author: Ahad Ha'am (Asher Ginsberg)
Ahad Ha'am's essays.description: Essays by a Hebrew writer from Odessa whose pen name means One of the People. Starting with This Is Not the Way in 1889, he criticised hasty settlement plans and reported frankly on problems in the Land of Israel. He argued that a Jewish centre there should first renew Jewish culture, language and values.
Ahad Ha'am's essays.significance: His ideas became known as cultural Zionism and offered an alternative to Herzl's focus on a state. They shaped Hebrew education and culture in Israel and are still debated by those who ask what makes a state Jewish.

Theodor Herzl, The Jewish State.author: Theodor Herzl
Theodor Herzl, The Jewish State.description: A short book by a Viennese journalist arguing that antisemitism would not disappear and that the answer was a state for the Jews. It sets out practical plans, including a society to lead the effort and a company to fund settlement. It was written in a clear, businesslike style.
Theodor Herzl, The Jewish State.significance: It launched political Zionism and led to the First Zionist Congress in Basel in 1897. Herzl is remembered as the visionary of the State of Israel, which was founded about fifty years later, and the book is still read as the starting point of the Zionist movement.

Sholem Aleichem, Tevye the Dairyman.author: Sholem Aleichem
Sholem Aleichem, Tevye the Dairyman.description: A series of stories in which Tevye, a poor and talkative dairyman, tells the author about his life and his daughters. Each daughter's choice of husband tests his faith and his traditions as the modern world reaches his village. The stories are funny and sad, full of misquoted scripture and quiet courage.
Sholem Aleichem, Tevye the Dairyman.significance: Tevye became one of the best-loved characters in Yiddish literature. The stories inspired the 1964 musical Fiddler on the Roof, through which millions around the world came to picture the vanished world of the shtetl.

The Chofetz Chaim, Mishnah Berurah.author: Yisrael Meir Kagan (the Chofetz Chaim)
The Chofetz Chaim, Mishnah Berurah.description: A six-volume commentary on the section of the Shulchan Aruch that covers daily life, prayer, Sabbath and festivals. It gathers the views of earlier authorities and gives clear rulings. Its author was known as the Chofetz Chaim after an earlier book he wrote on the laws of gossip and harmful speech.
The Chofetz Chaim, Mishnah Berurah.significance: It became the standard guide to daily Jewish practice for Ashkenazi Jews, and is relied on by many to this day. It is studied in yeshivas and study groups worldwide and is often printed alongside the Shulchan Aruch itself.

Hayim Nahman Bialik's poems.author: Hayim Nahman Bialik
Hayim Nahman Bialik's poems.description: Poems ranging from tender lyrics about nature and childhood to fierce national poetry. The best known, In the City of Slaughter, was written after the Kishinev pogrom of 1903 and attacks both the cruelty of the attackers and the helplessness of the victims. Bialik also wrote for children and helped collect Jewish legends.
Hayim Nahman Bialik's poems.significance: He is remembered as Israel's national poet and did much to show that Hebrew could carry modern poetry. In the City of Slaughter helped spur Jewish self-defence groups, and his poems are still taught in Israeli schools.

Eliezer Ben-Yehuda, Dictionary of the He.author: Eliezer Ben-Yehuda
Eliezer Ben-Yehuda, Dictionary of the He.description: A huge dictionary of Hebrew covering words from all periods, from the Bible to modern times, with sources and translations into other languages. Ben-Yehuda also coined new words for everyday modern life. The work was finished decades after his death in 1922 and filled seventeen volumes.
Eliezer Ben-Yehuda, Dictionary of the He.significance: It was a backbone of the revival of Hebrew as a spoken language, the effort for which Ben-Yehuda is best known. Today it is remembered as a symbol of the remarkable rebirth of Hebrew in the Land of Israel.

S. Ansky, The Dybbuk.author: S. Ansky
S. Ansky, The Dybbuk.description: A play about a young woman possessed by the spirit of her dead beloved, a poor scholar who had been promised to her before she was matched with a richer groom. It is set in a Hasidic world of mysticism and ends with an exorcism. Ansky drew on folklore gathered on his expeditions to the towns of Eastern Europe.
S. Ansky, The Dybbuk.significance: First staged in 1920, soon after Ansky died, it became the most famous play of the Yiddish theatre. A Hebrew version helped make the name of the Habima theatre, and the play is still performed, filmed and adapted today.

Rav Kook, Orot.author: Abraham Isaac Kook (Rav Kook)
Rav Kook, Orot.description: A collection of short, poetic writings by the first Ashkenazi Chief Rabbi of the Land of Israel, edited by his son. Its title means Lights. It presents the return to the Land of Israel and even the work of secular pioneers as part of a larger spiritual rebirth of the Jewish people.
Rav Kook, Orot.significance: It became a foundation of religious Zionism and its belief that the modern return to Zion has religious meaning. Controversial in its day, it still shapes religious Zionist thought and education in Israel and is studied closely in many yeshivas there.

Martin Buber, I and Thou.author: Martin Buber
Martin Buber, I and Thou.description: A short book of philosophy written in a poetic style. It contrasts two ways of relating to the world: treating others as objects to use, and meeting them as a whole person in true dialogue. Buber argues that every real meeting with another points towards a meeting with God.
Martin Buber, I and Thou.significance: It became one of the most influential works of religious thought of the 20th century, read by Jews and Christians alike. Its ideas about dialogue and genuine meeting between people still shape thinking in religion, education, psychology and therapy.

The Hertz Chumash.author: Joseph H. Hertz (Chief Rabbi)
The Hertz Chumash.description: An edition of the Five Books of Moses with the weekly readings from the Prophets, the Hebrew text, an English translation and a detailed commentary. It was edited by Joseph Hertz, Chief Rabbi of the British Empire. The commentary draws on traditional and modern scholarship and defends the Bible against critics of its day.
The Hertz Chumash.significance: For decades it sat in the pews of most English-speaking synagogues and taught generations of worshippers about the Torah. Though largely replaced by newer editions, it is fondly remembered as a classic of Anglo-Jewish life.

Mordecai Kaplan, Judaism as a Civilizati.author: Mordecai Kaplan
Mordecai Kaplan, Judaism as a Civilizati.description: A long study by an American rabbi and teacher that describes Judaism as the evolving civilisation of the Jewish people, including religion but also language, culture, art and community. It argues that Judaism must adapt to modern life and that Jewish community centres should be the heart of Jewish life.
Mordecai Kaplan, Judaism as a Civilizati.significance: It became the founding text of Reconstructionist Judaism and influenced American Jewish life far beyond that movement. Its idea of Judaism as a civilisation, shared by believers and non-believers alike, is still widely discussed today.

Gershom Scholem, Major Trends in Jewish.author: Gershom Scholem
Gershom Scholem, Major Trends in Jewish.description: A book based on lectures given in New York in 1938 by a scholar from the Hebrew University in Jerusalem. It traces Jewish mysticism from its early forms through the Zohar and Kabbalah to the false messiah Sabbatai Zevi and Hasidism. It uses careful historical study of manuscripts and sources.
Gershom Scholem, Major Trends in Jewish.significance: It turned Kabbalah from a neglected subject into a serious academic field. Later scholars have challenged some of its views, but it remains a classic starting point for anyone studying Jewish mysticism and Jewish intellectual history.

Anne Frank, The Diary of a Young Girl.author: Anne Frank
Anne Frank, The Diary of a Young Girl.description: The diary of a Jewish teenager who hid with her family and others in a secret annex in Amsterdam for over two years during the Nazi occupation. She writes about daily life in hiding, her hopes, her growing up and the people around her. Her father Otto, the only one of the group to survive, had it published after the war.
Anne Frank, The Diary of a Young Girl.significance: It is the most widely read book about the Holocaust and has been translated into many languages. Anne died in Bergen-Belsen in 1945, and her diary remains for many readers a first and personal encounter with the Holocaust.

Primo Levi, If This Is a Man.author: Primo Levi
Primo Levi, If This Is a Man.description: A memoir by an Italian Jewish chemist from Turin who was deported to Auschwitz in 1944. It describes life in the camp with calm, precise and thoughtful prose, looking at how people kept or lost their humanity. It is also published in English as Survival in Auschwitz.
Primo Levi, If This Is a Man.significance: It is one of the most important accounts of the Holocaust and is read in schools across the world. Levi went on to become a celebrated writer, and the book is valued for its clarity and moral insight.

Abraham Joshua Heschel, The Sabbath.author: Abraham Joshua Heschel
Abraham Joshua Heschel, The Sabbath.description: A short book on the meaning of the Sabbath by a rabbi and thinker born in Warsaw who later taught in New York. It contrasts a world focused on space and things with a Judaism focused on holiness in time. It describes the Sabbath as a palace in time, a weekly rest from the pursuit of possessions.
Abraham Joshua Heschel, The Sabbath.significance: It became a modern classic of Jewish spiritual writing, read across all streams of Judaism and beyond. It still shapes how many people think about rest, time and the value of stepping back from work.

Isaac Bashevis Singer, Gimpel the Fool a.author: Isaac Bashevis Singer
Isaac Bashevis Singer, Gimpel the Fool a.description: A collection of short stories by a Warsaw-born writer who settled in New York. The title story, translated into English by Saul Bellow, is about a simple baker in a shtetl who is tricked by everyone but keeps his faith and goodness. Other stories feature demons, folk beliefs and the lost world of Polish Jewry.
Isaac Bashevis Singer, Gimpel the Fool a.significance: The English translation of Gimpel the Fool brought Singer to a wide audience. In 1978 he won the Nobel Prize in Literature, the only writer in Yiddish to do so, and his stories are still widely read.

Leon Uris, Exodus.author: Leon Uris
Leon Uris, Exodus.description: A long historical novel by an American writer about the struggle to found the State of Israel. It follows characters through the Holocaust, the voyage of refugee ships and the fight for independence. Its hero, Ari Ben Canaan, became a model of the bold Israeli pioneer. It was turned into a famous 1960 film starring Paul Newman.
Leon Uris, Exodus.significance: It became a worldwide bestseller and shaped how many outside Israel, especially in America, pictured the country's founding. In the Soviet Union, where it was banned, it was secretly copied and passed around among Jews, inspiring many to seek to emigrate.

Elie Wiesel, Night.author: Elie Wiesel
Elie Wiesel, Night.description: A short memoir of a teenage boy deported with his family from the town of Sighet to Auschwitz in 1944. It describes the loss of his family, the camps and a death march, and his struggle with faith. A longer Yiddish version came first, followed by a shorter French version that was translated into English.
Elie Wiesel, Night.significance: It became one of the most widely read books about the Holocaust and is taught in schools around the world. Wiesel became a leading voice for Holocaust memory and received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1986.

S. Y. Agnon, Only Yesterday.author: S. Y. Agnon
S. Y. Agnon, Only Yesterday.description: A long novel about Isaac Kumer, a young man who leaves Galicia for the Land of Israel during the Second Aliyah in the early 20th century. It follows him between Jaffa and Jerusalem, and between secular pioneers and religious communities. A side story about a stray dog named Balak is one of its most famous parts.
S. Y. Agnon, Only Yesterday.significance: It is often called Agnon's greatest novel and a central work of modern Hebrew literature. In 1966 Agnon became the first Hebrew writer to win the Nobel Prize in Literature, and the novel is still studied in Israeli schools and universities.
